items.title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
items.content:
When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course.  
      In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods  (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge.
 The AI Transition  
      My journey on AI started with a selfish and narrow intent, which was to evaluate an investment I had made in Nvidia in 2018, for reasons entirely unrelated to AI. I thought that Nvidia, at the time, was a innovative chip company with more pricing power than many in its peer group, and felt that it was undervalued, given its prospects. While the stock outperformed my portfolio early on, it was the ChatGPT debut on November 30, 2022, and the subsequent AI buzz that put its stock price on steroids. That left me with a challenge, albeit a welcome one, of deciding whether I should continue to hold on to a stock that had already become a twenty-bagger or sell some or all of it. Since much of Nvidia's supersized success was being propelled by AI demand, that required me to take my first look at how big the AI market would be, and how well Nvidia was positioned to take advantage of that market. If you have read my multiple posts on Nvidia over the last three years, you may be aware that I sold all my shares in the company in four installments, with the last sale happening earlier this year. As many of you have been quick to point out, my decision to gradually decrease my Nvidia position has led me to leave money on the table, but I have no regrets. 
 The Players 
      In the process of trying to understand AI and disentangle the many players in the AI space. I break them down broadly into four groups:

 AI Suppliers: While AI is viewed as a technology business, we have learned over the last few years that it is much more capital intensive than any other tech endeavor in history. The data centers and infrastructure that are needed to power AI agents and models has created a surge in demand for ingredients. The biggest portion of the cost, at least so far, has been on high-powered  chips, with Nvidia claiming a lion's share, and enough left over demand for other chip companies to benefit. This infrastructure build out has increased demand for electrical equipment, with power and real estate companies also gaining as data centers get built. AI Builders: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, four companies that were part of FANGAM, the acronym that predates the Mag Seven, bought into the AI hope, and joined by a handful of other players (Oracle, Coreweave), they have invested hundreds of billions of dollars into AI cap ex (data centers and infrastructure). The market cut these hyperscalers slack early on, rewarding them for their capital spending, even though that spending was denting profitability at these companies and demolishing cash flows, and part of the AI trade question has been whether the market is running out of patience, waiting for payoff. AI Products : In the last two years, companies which are on the frontlines of creating AI products and services, have became the focal point of investors, albeit in the private investing world, with talk of public offerings pricing them in the trillions of dollars. SpaceX became the first of these to list, but Anthropic's IPO is imminent and OpenAI will join, sooner rather than later. There are  other companies (Palantir is the most prominent), albeit only a handful, that are  have made AI a central component of the products and services they sell, but that number will be added to, as private businesses in the space go public. AI Customers : There is a fourth group, perhaps more critical than any of the above, that will determine the value creation potential and long-term standing of this business, and that includes all of the potential customers, individual as well as businesses, for AI products and services. While the premise for AI hype is that its reach (both in terms of numbers and monetization) will be huge, it is undeniable, even if you are an AI diehard, that there is little of substance to show at the moment. Even if you take the ARR numbers that are being leaked by the lead players, the collective revenues from AI products and services right now is about $250 billion, a small number relative to what has been invested in the space. The entire AI ecosystem is built on the premise that this group will become much larger, both in terms of reach across businesses and money spent in the trillions of dollars. The companies in all of these groups can be classified as being in the AI business, but they generate value in very different ways from that business.

 The Linkages 
   There are links that hold these groups together, and I have tried to capture those linkages and how they play out as revenues, expenses and earnings in each group:

 This simple, and perhaps even over-simplistic, breakdown of AI does, in my view, provide a good starting point for understanding why their interests and market pricing is more likely to diverge in the future, as the business takes form.    The linkages between the AI groups come from three core transactions between these groups that determine not just their current earnings but also their long term value propositions:

 Building the AI infrastructure: The  AI builders are spending the money building the infrastructure and much of it is being legitimately classified as capital expenditures, though there is a discussion to be had about the life of that infrastructure. The reason that the investment life matters is that it determines the amortization schedule for the AI cap ex, and consequently the negative impact on earnings in the current year; the free cashflows  are lower since they take a direct hit from the cap ex. The suppliers report these same capital expenditures as revenues in the current year, and when netted out against their operating costs, increase earnings at these companies. I wrote about how the net effect of the infrastructure buildout has been an increase in aggregate earnings at US companies in the last year, and has supported stock prices, even as interest rates have soared. Leasing the AI infrastructure: The AI architecture, once built, is leased out by the builders to the businesses that use the data centers to create and support the products and services they offer. The builders report the lease payments as revenues , allowing them to earn a return back on their infrastructure build, but for the AI product and service businesses, these payments are either operating expenses, if annually reset, or financial expenses , if structured as contractual commitments over many years; the latter will create imputed interest expenses and depreciation. Creating and selling AI products: Using the leased AI architecture, AI product and service businesses create products and services that they sell to consumers (individual and enterprise) and record the payment they receive, from either subscription or usage-based models, as revenues . With the LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic), these products are AI agents and frontier models where users pay either in subscriptions or based upon usage, and net of the costs of creating these products, hopefully into profits.  The linkages between the companies in the AI ecosystem described in the section above are operating linkages that are part and parcel of doing business, but there are financial linkages, though, the motives for which I will examine later in this post, that are messier. In particular,  AI companies have funded each other, with both equity and debt. Microsoft and Nvidia are shareholders in OpenAI, Alphabet and Amazon in Anthropic and Nvidia has also provided financial backstops for data centers being built out. These financial cross holdings create accounting noise (with mark ups of equity investments reported as earnings) and contribute to opacity.

 The Timing of Benefits 
      Given that AI infrastructure can take years to come online, there will be timing differences across the groups, in terms of seeing the benefits from their business models, with AI suppliers being the first to see revenues and profits, followed by AI builders, with AI product & service businesses generally being last to see profitability.
 1. Hope and Hype           
     In the first phases of a disruption, the visions of a huge market often drive actions on the part of all of the AI groups, but the way they play out and how they show up in results will vary: 

 The suppliers of the ingredients that go into AI infrastructure will be the first to see tangible benefits as the s pending on AI architecture shows up immediately as revenues in income statement and as incremental profit s.  For AI builders, no matter how merited the build-up (in terms of delivering value over time), the immediate effect on both earnings and cash flows will be negative . The reason the earnings effects has been muted with AI is because the biggest AI infrastructure investors (Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon) have earnings and cashflows from legacy businesses and the cloud businesses (thus playing a role asiAI suppliers) that have provided a buffer, but the free cash flow impact has been real. For companies in the AI product group, which are nascent businesses, t here will be little to show in terms of revenues , since neither the infrastructure nor the products are ready to go. With R&D and employee compensation expenses, they will be money-losing machines. For AI, the hope and hype phase was most pronounced in 2023 and 2024, and not surprisingly, the biggest surge in market capitalization during the period was at Nvidia, as its chips became the essential ingredient to get investments going.

 2. Investment Buildup 
      In this phase, the AI infrastructure building continues at a torrid pace, but portions of it are complete and ready for use, and the consequences again will vary for the groups involved:

 As growth in AI infrastructure continues, AI suppliers will continue to see growth in revenues and profit from the continued building , though growth rates will come down with scale. In addition, new entrants may start to compete on prices, reducing pricing power at least for some of the supplier groups. For Ai builders, the portion of the AI that is ready to use can be leased out, allowing for a monetization of at least a portion of the AI investment. Since the investment continues to increase, and much of it is still not operational, on measures like return on capital, the AI buildup investment will not measure up. Markets will often be willing to forgive, at least with managers that they trust, on the assumption that things will get better over time. As AI infrastructure comes online, AI product companies can start generating products and services , and to the extent that they are growing from small scale, growth rates can be exponential. Those revenues though will generally be dwarfed by expenses from product development, continued research, and employee compensation, leaving the companies with large losses. With AI users,  a mix of early adopters and experimenters, in a subset of industries where AI is viewed as having the most promise, will emerge. Given AI’s strengths, software businesses were among the first to be exposed to AI products, with consequences for competitive position and profitability, but AI agents also have found a foothold in white collar businesses. Through much of 2025, AI suppliers continued to benefit, AI builders invested hundreds of billions of dollars in AI cap ex, seemingly without much pushback, the product companies drew attention with frontier models that dazzled users with their mix of power, albeit with rough edges, and markets continued to reward them all, based on its perception of market potential.

 3. Business Building 
     A big end market notwithstanding, business building is hard and in this phase it is inevitable that questions will turn to unit economics, economies of scale and eventual profitability, with each group facing different degrees of questioning.

 By this stage, AI suppliers should have fully formed business models , but revenue growth rates will ease, as new infrastructure spend becomes smaller, at least on relative terms. As builders try to develop cheaper supply sources, either by bringing some of it in-house or by looking at competitors, margins will start to compress, and you will see some suppliers focus on the infrastructure replenishment/replacement market, rather than on new infrastructure. Since markets are forward-looking, the pricing of these companies will reflect expectations of lower growth and the companies will look cheap on a pricing basis (low PE ratios, low EV multiples), relative to their history. As more infrastructure becomes operational, AI builders will begin to see more revenues and earnings from existing investments, but the magnitude will depend largely on whether demand from AI product companies is running ahead of capacity (good for revenues and earnings) or behind (bad for revenues and earnings). As returns on invested capital pick up, markets will make their own assessments of whether they will end up adding or destroying value, and reassess the pricing of these companies accordingly. AI product companies will jockey for position in the market, looking for ways to differentiate their products and preserve pricing power. With compute power being a key driver of both AI model power and growth in revenues, AI companies will try to not only get more AI infrastructure under control, but, if it is scarce, lock it for the long term. In the aftermath, AI product companies with a duration problem, where AI compute commitments are locked up long term, while their revenue streams are still in their formative phase and subject to short term volatility. Again, the forward-looking nature of markets implies that the pricing of these companies will look high, relative to current operating numbers, but that pricing will be volatile, as markets reassess prospects. AI users will find themselves on the receiving end of sales pitches for AI products and services, with the key selling point being improved productivity, with the warning included that not buying these products will put them at a disadvantage, relative to competitors.  For AI to find its business feet, you need the customer base for AI products and services to become both wider (cutting across many different industries) and deeper (where customers spend far more on AI, on a repeat basis).  There are three broad scenarios that can unfold.  The first is that AI products and services work much better than expected , and that the demand for these products runs ahead of expectations. In this scenario, AI product companies will benefit first, since they will see growing revenues and higher pricing power, which create the unit economics and economies of scale for escalating profits, but the benefits will ripple to the AI builders, allowing them to increase capacity, which in turn will lift AI supplers. The second is that AI products and services work about as well as expected , with demand matching up to expectations. In this case, AI product companies should, at least in the aggregate, hold their own, but as with any competitive business, some will gain at the expense of others. There will be both business consequences, as weaker players drop out, and market implications, as the market adjusts the pricing for the survivors. The third is that AI products and services work less well than expected , with demand and monetization falling well below expectations. This will hurt not just the AI product companies who will struggle to meet revenue targets, but ripple through the other groups, as product companies either break or renegotiate compute commitments, hurting builders, who in turn, will shut down or abandon infrastructure capacity, creating pain for AI suppliers.

 Commonalities and Competing Interests 
     Even though the businesses in the AI space have very different business models, there is one common element that holds them together; the value of all of the players in the ecosystem ultimately will be determined by the size of the AI market and its profitability. As I noted in my earlier posts on AI, if the end market for AI products and services is small, because of the imperfections as AI tools, regulatory restrictions or limited reach, the entire AI ecosystem (builders, suppliers and product businesses will all feel the pain. Conversely, if AI delivers on its promise as a powerful productivity tool that works across many businesses, all of them benefit, albeit in different forms and different degrees. If history is a guide, it is the product companies that will be the primary benefactors, but the central role of compute power in the AI business may give AI builders and suppliers more of a share. In addition, if one of the groups faces growth and survival challenges, those pains will spread into the other groups as well. That may explain why you see so much circular financing in the AI ecosystem, where financially better- positioned and stronger players like Nvidia invest in or offer financing guarantees to weaker players, either to ensure survival or to provide an impetus for continued investment spending.
      Those common interests notwithstanding, these businesses also have competing agendas, and decisions and actions that affect one group negatively can create benefit for others. Thus, if AI builders choose to build too much infrastructure, too quickly, it will hurt them and their shareholders, but that overbuilding will be a bonanza for the AI suppliers, as chips, equipment, power and real estate players all benefit from the overbuilding. Once built, it is in the AI builders' interests to lease out the infrastructure for longer periods than merited, locking in their revenue streams, but for the AI product companies, those long term commitments can increase default risk. In short, as the AI business matures, I would expect these competing interests will often overwhelm the common interests, creating divergence. 
      For much of AI's early existence, the commonalities have overwhelmed the competing interests, with the hope of a large market for AI products and services pushing up market pricing for all of the groups, with AI chip companies like Nvidia being rewarded for the expected growth in AI architecture, hyperscale

items.title: The Anthropic Feedback Loop: The Cost of Capital Delusion and Diversion!
items.content:
I knew that my post on Anthropic would draw strong reactions, when I made it public last week. I did mention in the course of the post that I have no interest in selling my estimate of value to the rest of the world, both because I don't own the high ground here and because it is meant to guide my decisions, not yours. That is why I made my model open to changes that you can make to my story and inputs, and while you have to trust my mechanics, I tried to carry your inputs into value. Much of the pushback I have received has been thoughtful and productive, some of it has been emotional (either from people who love Anthropic or from those who would not touch it with a ten-foot pole) and some of it, especially on the cost of capital, reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and just basic business sense. I plan to play devil's advocate with my own valuation, looking at my story inputs, and ranking them in order of fragility, partly to stress-test my value estimate and partly to reinforce some corporate finance first principles, and then move on to your feedback and what I take away from it.
 Playing Devil's Advocate: A self-critique of my Anthropic valuation 
     Since I posted my valuation only a week ago, rather than rehash how I approached the valuation and my end results, you can read the gory details in the post that accompanied it. I will start with a summary of the valuation, though, and then list  the parts of my story that I believe are most directly driving my value estimate on both magnitude (how much it is affecting value) and fragility (how uncertain I feel about the part).  
 The IPO Valuation 
     I did summarize my valuation of Anthropic in a figure in my original post, but since there was that much to compress into that picture, I will try a different format for the same here: 

 Download updated spreadsheet 

 If you check against my estimates from my earlier post, you will notice that the equity value at $1.45 trillion is slightly lower than my prior estimate of $1.475 trillion, as I adjusted the trailing 12-month revenue and operating income numbers to include the just-leaked third quarter numbers. Note that replacing the third quarter revenues from 2025 with the third quarter revenues of 2026 raises the base revenues, and since I still believe that the revenues for the coming twelve months will stay at my original estimate of about $100 billion, the growth rate in revenues in year 1 has been adjusted down to deliver that result. This reframing allows me to add a few details that I might have glossed over in my last post, as well as correct errors (none of which thankfully changed by value estimate:  

 Value per share : Though I have a share count, created by adding the shares reported as outstanding in the balance sheet to the restricted shares granted to employees, that share count will change before the public offering, as bankers adjust it to deliver on a per share value that they believe will make the company more "sellable". I will revisit this number, and update it when the company does (and it has to, before setting an offering price), but it should not change the aggregate value of equity. Cost of capital choices: I used a 9.74% cost of capital which incorporates risky technology cost of equity and a cost of debt based on a BB+ rating for the company, putting the company at close to the 90th percentile of US companies in 2026. I know that some of you felt this was too low, and I will come back to address what a cost of capital can and cannot do for you in valuation, later in this post, and why I don't think that this is the input that most moves the valuation. Compute commitments : I wish that Anthropic had created a table in their prospectus, where they specifically listed total commitments, both contractual and total, by year, similar to the table that they have for purchase commitments. Instead, they have sprayed content commitment numbers in the text, with little detail on timing and contractual standing, which results in differences of opinion in what those commitments are., with estimates ranging from $400 billion to $800 billion, with no clarity on timing or contractual terms. In my valuation, my estimate of contractual commitments results in an aggregated value of just over $450 billion and a present value of about $373 billion. It is possible that these numbers will need revisiting as details emerge of these commitments, but this will remain a long term issue for anyone valuing or pricing the company. To offer an imperfect analogy, I struggle with dealing with content commitments at Netflix, whenever I value the company, and especially so in the early years, when the entire Netflix library was leased or rented from content providers. Dilution Risk: Anthropic, like many young companies, has used its equity as currency, paying employees with restricted stock and options, and used it as an add-on to borrow money in the form of convertible bonds. In addition, if the company needs to raise capital in future years, it will have to issue additional shares for that purpose, and the larger its ambitions, the greater these issuances will be. When valuing Anthropic, there is no escaping this dilution overhang, and here is how it is incorporated into the value per share. With stock-based compensation, I valued the equity options (at their option value, rather than exercise value) and netted that number ($472 million) from my estimated equity value to get to value of equity in common stock; I also included the restricted shares as part of my share count to compute value per share. With the convertible debt, I have assumed that the marked-to-market number (it was the marking to market that created the $72 billion hit to earnings in 2026) is close to fair value, and subtracting it out will remove the conversion option from the equity. The future share issuances are to fund negative free cashflows , and since those negative cashflows are already weighing down my present value, there is no need to add the shares issued to the share count; adding it will be double counting. If you are surprised that adding the third quarter numbers did not move my value by much, it is because it was an open secret that Anthropic's third quarter revenue growth had slowed and I had already incorporated that into my valuation story.

 Value Drivers 
      The equity value that I obtain for Anthropic is close to the lower end of the offering price estimates, but as I noted at the time that I posted it, and will reinforce again now, it is a function of not just my upbeat story about the company, but also one about how the AI products and services market will evolve over time. To the question that some posed about whether I was concerned that I could be wrong, of course I am, but as I will argue in the next section, I cannot let that concern paralyze me. I would, of course, rather be right than wrong, but I am trying to forecast the future, and it is a guarantee that I will be wrong. That said, I am more uncertain and exposed on some parts of my story line than others, and here is how I would rank them for Anthropic, from most critical to less so:

 Target Revenues: If I were forced to pick one variable around which my valuation revolves the most, it is my estimate of the target revenues for Anthropic , which I estimate to reach a trillion dollars in ten years. Not only would this put them at or close to the top of all companies, in terms of total annual revenues, but they will also be sharing that grouping with companies like Amazon and Walmart that deliver on scale, but at the expense of margins. The revenue assumption is also inextricably linked to not only what you think AI agents and products can do, but also how demand for these will be monetized. In addition, there is a company-specific component to this story, where Anthropic emerges as a winner in the premium portion of the AI market. capturing a dominant market share, with pricing power.

 The fragility of the target revenue assumption comes from it being susceptible to any of the parts failing, and if a part fails, revenues will end up below a trillion, and perhaps significantly so. That, in turn, will have ripple effects on the other parts of your story and inputs, with lower revenue growth pushing down margins, creating idle compute power and increasing the risk of failure. 
 Governance : I did use harsh words to describe the governance structure at Anthropic in my last post, describing the combination of its structure as a public benefit corporation and a voting share concoction that leaves founders in control , no matter how much capital the company raises in equity markets, as a red flag. I did get some pushback from some arguing that this is a good feature, not a bad one, since these are smart people who understand AI better than anyone else in the world. Even if you accept these views  I would still argue, perhaps even more forcefully, that concentrating power in the hands of founders is a bad idea, and here is why. Anthropic has a plausible or even probable pathways to business riches, but those pathways come with setbacks (technological, regulatory, competitive), and you need management that can respond quickly and decisively, sometimes abandoning existing policies. For the latter to happen, you often need outsiders, not as immersed or even as informed on the technology front, but with different  backgrounds and experiences, to call attention to management missteps and push for change. I don't know any of the founders of Anthropic, and this may be unfair, but they seem to share a common worldview and operate in an echo chamber. My concern, as an investor, would be that they will not see changes occurring in business economics, and even if they do, be unable to or unwilling to adapt to a changing environment, and for Anthropic, that may be fatal. Profitability : My story for Anthropic is that it will not only be able to deliver operating profits soon, but do so on a sustained basis, with a target operating margin of 32.5% (before taking the regulatory risk haircut). Implicit in my profit story are assumptions about pricing power, the unit economics of the AI business and economies of scale and each is breakable:

 One of the most frequent critiques I received in responses to my Anthropic valuation is that this is a business without moats, and while I agree that moats matter, I am not sure that I go along with the notion that this business will get commoditized. The truth in technology is that unlike consumer products or old economy companies, where the moats take the form of brand names, patents or cost advantages, the companies that win find ways to make their products stickier to their customers, where stickiness implies that customers will not switch to alternatives, even if these alternatives are technically superior and cheaper. I recognize that Anthropic has work to do in creating stickiness, but I can visualize ways in which Claude agents, twinned with client data on customers and employees, can become sticky, allowing the company to preserve its pricing power and market share.
 Continuing investment needs : While much of the focus on Anthropic has been on their compute commitments, disclosed (loosely) in their prospectus, my valuation of Anthropic is driven by expectations of what those commitments will look like over time, and especially if my growth story for the company comes into fruition. Delivering a trillion dollars of revenues will require Anthropic to not just maintain and replenish the compute power that is has already locked down, but add to that power over time. Implicit in my story line for the company, where the company is able to add this compute power at lower costs (reflecting declining chip prices) and in time, is the assumption that the compute power story moves along smoothly, working through resource constraints and pushback: 

 If you have been tracking news stories about data centers, it seems clear that building new data centers is getting more difficult, as local communities push back, and politicians realize that opposing them is a net vote winner. 
 Regulatory risk : You may find this surprising, but risk, in my story, is not as critical as my first four inputs, partly because it is determined by shifts in operating variables. Put simply, Anthropic will become riskier, if revenues do not measure up to expectations and the pathway to profitability becomes rockier, making it more an output than an input variable. I know that for some of you, the cost of capital of 9.74% is the main stumbling block, but I will provide a more cohesive (and hopefully) more persuasive argument of why it is not as critical to value as you may believe it is. I also know that for others, the notion of a money-losing company borrowing hundreds of billions, either directly as debt or through contractual commitments, creates a failure risk probability that is so high that the rest of the valuation is moot. I agree with you on the general argument that some players in the AI ecosystem, such as Coreweave, have abandoned corporate finance first principles and risk bankruptcy, but Anthropic is no Coreweave, especially if you consider that most of its debt is in contractual commitments spread out over time and that it will have a cash balance large enough to cover its first few years of those commitments. It is on the regulatory risk front that I worry the most about being wrong, because regulatory risk is as much driven by politics as it is driven by economics. You could be one major election away from onerous regulations on AI, where unlike my base case, where those regulations cost you only a small slice of your operating profits, they take a major bite out of revenues and profits.  
 In sum, not only will I be wrong on any of my key inputs, but being wrong on one (especially target revenues) will cause me to be wrong (in the same direction) on my other inputs, causing value to shift more dramatically in response. 
 Investment Followthrough 
     At this point, you are probably why, if I am this uncertain about a company's future, I would even consider investing in it and it is a question that I have pondered as long as I have been an investor. Uncertainty is a feature of investing, no matter what you invest in, with the differences across investments lying in how much uncertainty you face, rather than whether you face. There are four responses that an investor can take to uncertainty: 

 Ignore it : There are investors who are capable of ignoring uncertainty and going in fully even on the most uncertain investments. They are able to do so because they are far less risk averse than the rest of us and are willing to live with the consequences of investments (and their portfolios) blowing up. They are more gamblers than investors, but with good instincts and timing, gamblers can get wealthy too. Avoid it: If you completely want to avoid uncertainty, you cannot invest in equities, corporate bonds, which have risk of default, and even treasury bonds, which have price risk from shifting interest rates. Unless you want to hold just hold cash, you have to therefore decide what your threshold for risk is, and stay within that threshold. In conventional value investing, that would lead you to restrict your investments to companies with assets in place (captured in book value) and earning power from those assets (high current earnings and cash flows) and stay away from growth companies, since growth is "speculative" and therefore risky. While I understand the impulse, this choice comes with a cost, which is that your portfolio will be almost entirely invested in mature and declining companies, with no growth companies in emergent technology.  Margin of Safety: The third approach to dealing with uncertainty also borrows from conventional value investing and imposing a margin of safety, where you will buy a stock only if its price is less than your value estimate by a margin (20%, 30%, 40%) that you specify. While your inclination, if your risk averse, is to keep increasing your margin of safety, it is worth remembering that like almost everything else in investing, it creates a trade off between type 1 errors (where having a higher margin of safety protects you from the losses of investing in stocks that you should not be investing in) and type 2 errors (where that higher margin of safety keeps you from investing in good stocks that you should be holding):

 The question of whether you should have a margin of safety, and if so, how large it should be, will be a function not only of how many opportunities you see in the market, relative to your portfolio size, and how much cash you have in your portfolio (with larger cash balances suggesting that you should lower your margin of safety).
 Law of large numbers : If I had a million dollars in investable funds, would I invest that entire amount in Anthropic, even if it trades at well below my assessed value? The answer would be no, given the uncertainties associated with the future of the company, but that answer would change if my portfolio became less concentrated, since its performance would be less a function of any individual company's performance (good or bad). In effect, I am using the law of large numbers as an ally to not only reduce my risk exposure to individual companies, but also as a basis for making investments in far riskier stocks than I would be otherwise inclined to invest in. As you assess your story and valuation of Anthropic, it is crucial that you frame the question that you are trying to answer with your analysis. Is it whether you should buy or sell short Anthropic, as a stand-alone investment or are you looking at Anthropic as an add-on to an existing portfolio? If it is the latter, how concentrated (across stocks and sectors) is your existing portfolio? The answers will vary, as a consequence.

 Keeping the feedback loop open: Your pushback on my valuation 
   In the days since I posted my Anthropic valuation on multiple platforms (X, LinkedIn, Google, Substack and YouTube), I have heard from many of you, and in the interests of keeping the feedback loop alive, I did a breakdown of two statistics - the percent of people who thought that I was over valuing and undervaluing Anthropic, and among the majority who thought I was overvaluing, their reasons for disagreement. I used the Google shared spreadsheet that I created last week, where some of you were kind enough to enter your story/inputs and value for the company, and here is what you found: 

 Clearly, a lot of people disagree with my assessment, with more feeling that I have over valued Anthropic, rather than under value the company, with the crowd assessment of its value closer to $1 trillion, rather than $1.5 trillion. I also used your inputs from the shared sheet, as well as a reading of the comments on my valuation, across platforms, to see the source of your disagreement, especially if you believed that I have overvalued the company. 

 Among those who disagreed with me, the reasoning varied, but I was disappointed, albeit not surprised, that the biggest single reason outside of "my gut tells me that Anthropic is worth nothing" was a judgment that my cost of capital estimate for the company (9.74%) was much too low. I was disappointed because I don't think that the cost of capital is at the center of the DCF universe (and I used words to that effect in my original valuation) but the lack of surprise at its prominence comes from observing appraisers and analysts obsess over this number, often without understanding what it is designed to measure and without a frame of reference (as to what a reasonable value for it is), and using it as a receptacle for their hopes, fears and fantasies.
