items.title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
items.content:
I am a dabbler, by nature, moving on from topic to topic, but this year, I have spent more time than usual on AI, but that is because it seems to be part of almost every business or economy related story. I tried to value SpaceX ahead of and after the filing of the prospectus for its initial public offering before moving on to the question of whether it and OpenAI and Anthropic should be part of the S&P 500 index . I started my analysis of how AI would affect the rest of us , from doomsday to do-nothing scenarios, largely in response to Citrini and Citadel reports on the topic. in August 2026, I took my first big picture look at AI as a business, which I titled its bar mitzvah moment, with a look at its potential market, business economics and moats. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing.  In early October, I looked at how the massive investments in AI are playing out in the aggregate earnings , cashflows and invested capital at US companies, and why it is contributing to holding the market intact, in the face of rising rates. Just last week, I argued that both Anthropic and OpenAI would be priced , rather than valued, for their initial public offerings, using what I called buzzy metrics (like annualized run rates) and promised that I would try to value the company, when it filed its prospectus. On October 26, Anthropic filed its prospectus , and at the risk of being called hopelessly wrong by both bulls and bears, I will try to value the company, using what I see as its most likely pathway, while also leaving the door open for you to disagree with me, and pick your own pathways to valuing the company. 
 The Prospectus 
     Before I delve into the details of the S-1 filed by Anthropic, it is worth noting that at 416 pages, it is long and filled with distractions, as has become the case with almost every initial public offering in the last two decades. (I chronicled this trend in my post on the d isclosure dilemma , arguing that while filings have become longer, they have become less informative). The Anthropic IPO has useful information that both bulls and bears will spin to justify their priors, and in the section below, I look at key disclosures, broken down by valuation input into revenue growth, profitability, risk and reinvestment categories, from both an optimist (glass half full) and pessimist (glass half empty) perspective: 

 Revenue Growth and Composition : The good news in the revenue story is that the company has grown exponentially over the last year, with revenues in the first two quarters of this year about fourteen times as high as the revenues in the first two quarters of the last year, but the sobering news is that revenue growth slowed down in the third quarter of 2026, as OpenAI increased market share, compute capacity acted as a constraint and some enterprises moved to cheaper open source models. The good news on customer composition is that the number of enterprises that spend more than $1 million a year on Claude increased to 1900 , from less than a hundred a year ago, but the bad news is that the company still has concentrated revenues , with its top five customers accounting for 25% of revenues. 

 Operating and Net Profitability : In bad news, Anthropic reported an operating loss, corrected for non-cash and one-time charges, of over $ 8 billion, for  the first six months of the year. The actual loss reported was $80 billion, but $72 billion represented a non-cash charge, expensing the conversion option of the convertible bond. The good news, though, is that not only are the trend lines working in their favor, with the company claiming that it had an operating profit in the most recent quarter. The company is also delivering its revenues more efficiently over time, with all of its expenses decreasing as a percent of revenues across the quarters, with compute costs, its biggest cost,, decreasing from more than 250% of revenues to 48% of revenues, on a quarterly basis.

 Reinvestment for growth : AI agents are computing power hogs, and AI companies invest immense amounts in compute power. The financial statements in Anthropic's prospectus actually do not show this investment at the moment, with neither the cap ex in the statement of cash flow nor the debt (and invested capital) in the balance sheet showing substantial investment in compute power. Before you accuse Anthropic of hiding the truth (or worse), the company is open about its future compute power commitments, reporting hundreds of billions in compute commitments in future years. The good news is that Anthropic is now catching up with OpenAI, which had the lead on compute power, but the bad news is that this catching up has not been cheap, in terms of cost commitments in future years. It i s also worth noting that compute power will need to be renewed and reinvested in, and while chip costs (a key component) may come down, data centers, facing opposition from communities, may become more expensive. 

 Operating and Regulatory risk : Anthropic's argument is that its customers, once they adopt Claude models within their enterprises, will find that they become so integral to operations that they will not abandon them (making revenues sticky and the business less risky). That has not been fully tested yet, and it is entirely possible that spending on AI agents is cyclical and that companies will pull back in bad times. On the financing front, committing to hundreds of billons in compute, purchase and lease commitments exposes the firm to default risk (with a bond rating of BB+), but in response the company will argue that its access to new capital, as a publicly traded large market-cap company, will make this risk recede. In addition, its cash balance, already at $114 billion, and likely to be bulked up with another $100 billion from the IPO offering, will give them more than enough cash to cover commitments in the next few years. 
 Source for AI risks:  https://airisk.mit.edu  If I were to summarize the information that I obtained in the prospectus that is relevant to valuing the company, I would come up with the following (and neither Anthropic bulls nor bears will be happy with me):

 The company's revenues are growing quickly, and for at least of the subset of users that are its core customers, it is delivering on its promise. That said, the revenue growth rate is clearly coming down, as scale, competition and compute power constraints all work against the company, and the fact that Anthropic is so interconnected in both operating and financing practices with other big players in the AI game (the circularity that is often noted by critics) does lead to the potential for double counting and opacity. The expenses for Anthropic, across categories, are growing slower than revenues and that is helping reduce operating losses and putting the company on a glide path to not just profitability, but significant profitability. That said, notwithstanding one quarter's reported profits, the company is not quite there yet, and will require significant revenue growth to keep ahead of the expenses (from the compute power commitments) that will hit the income statement in future periods. The immense compute power commitments at Anthropic have not only allowed the company to lock in what it needs to deliver growth but are also largely responsible for the high gross profit margins reported by the company, because they have moved company's biggest expense from the variable to the fixed operating cost column. That has come at a cost, since this not only increases the company's operating leverage, but also will result in further commitments down the road, as compute power needs to be replenished and grown. Anthropic has built a buffer against risk in the form of a very large cash balance, which will be augmented after the IPO, and it is is possible that Anthropic's customers will become reliant on its products, making its revenue stickier.  However, it is exposed to risk on three dimensions - in operations, from high operating leverage, in financing, because of its contractual content cost commitments and on survival, since it is dependent on growth to meet its obligations. 
 Over the next few days, don't be surprised to see people make cases for and against Anthropic using their spin of the data in the prospectus. Neither side will be convinced, or convincing, and will emerge with their priors about Anthropic intact and reinforced. I think that too much time and effort is being spent on going through this prospectus, as if it contains the answers to every question you may have on AI, when, in truth, it is a snapshot of a young company that is evolving. This prospectus, at least in my view, is analogous to reviewing a report card for a kindergartner (a precocious and talented one perhaps, but still a kindergartner) and trying to determine how much, if any, to set into that child's college fund. 
     My one piece of advice, no matter which side of the optimist/pessimist divide you may fall on, is that you do not get sucked into conspiracy stories revolving around AI company cabals (where the hyper-scalers, chip maker and LLMs are all working at creating a mirage of AI success to fool investors) or accounting fraud. I agree that self interest is driving many of the actions that you observe in this space and that accountants sometimes use the discretion in accounting rules to make the numbers look more favorable for companies than they really are, but those are common problems across all companies, not just AI and Anthropic, and falling into the conspiracy rabbit holes effectively blocks you from even considering alternative explanations. 

 The Anthropic Valuation - Story and Numbers 
     The prospectus, with all of its disclosures, is still a document rooted in the past, and the value of a business lies in your expectations for the future. In this section, I am planning to leave the safety of the historical disclosures and embark on forecasting the future, knowing fully well that I am going to be wrong, and perhaps even massively wrong, in my attempts. At each step of the story, I will offer you a chance to disagree with my take, and provide your own, with the resulting change in inputs. I know that you are busy, but if you can humor me and play alone, we may both benefit from this exercise. 

 1. The Scaling Up Story 
     The value of Anthropic, and any of the other AI product and service companies that will come later, ultimately rests on how big you believe the AI products and services market will become, and what portion of that market you company will inhabit. I started on this discussion a couple of months ago in my assessment of AI as a business , and argued that the total market for AI products and services will depend on four assessments -  

 whether AI is a productivity   tool for employees or employee replacement , with the latter creating a larger market for its products and services. whether that employee displacement will be primarily at the top end (top quintile) of the wage scale or across the board , with the latter pushing up the total market. whether AI's impact will be concentrated in a few industry groups or across many or most industries , with the market expanding as AI's reach expands whether the AI disruption will be primarily in the United States and a few other geographies or global, with a global reach leading to a bigger market. I used the picture below to illustrate the range of total market outcomes:

 I believe that AI will have the power to disrupt some industries, and that its most powerful (and highest priced) models will displace white collar (and highly paid) employees, yielding an end market size of $5 trillion or greater for its products. In my view, and that is based on a very early reading of the AI business today, Anthropic is aiming for the premium portion of the market and looks like a leader in that portion of the market. The one emerging add on is Anthropic's ambition (made explicit in the prospectus) to be a competitor in a subset of the businesses that its agents are disrupting, with the pharmaceutical business emerging as a potential play. In effect, Anthropic Pharma, or whatever they choose to call it, will then use its agents to do drug research and testing, displacing the companies that currently provide this service, and reap at least a portion of the revenues from the drugs they develop.  With that story in place, I believe that it is plausible that Anthropic's revenues could approach a trillion dollars in a decade. For perspective, there is only no company in the world with more than a trillion in revenues today, with Amazon and Walmart sitting at around $700-$750 billion (albeit in current dollars and time). 
     Clearly, these are my views, and yours may be very different. If you are willing to play along, I would like you to make your own assessment and make your choice below:

 My choice is shaded black, and as you make your choice, pay more attention to the target revenues that you believe Anthropic will have in 2036 than to the compounded annual growth rate between years 2 and 5, which is just an input to get to your target revenues.

 2. The Profitability Story 
     There is clearly movement towards profitability in the prospectus, but where will the profit margins end up after Anthropic has gone through its growth pains? To estimate where margins will converge, it may help to start with the recognition that the AI product and service market, once established, is likely to have a mass market segment where AI agents and models, many of which may be open-sourced and less powerful, will compete for customers primarily on pricing, and a premium segment, where frontier models, many of which will remain closed models, powered by client data, dominate. The operating margins for the former are more likely to resemble those of business services (roughly 10%), whereas the operating margins for the latter will converge on the operating margins of enterprise software (close to 40% for the top quartile), with compute power and R&D becoming the reinvestment needed to deliver these products. 
     Anthropic is targeting the premium market, as reflected not only in its current revenue breakdown, with almost 80% from enterprises paying based on usage, but also in its focus on using its newly acquired compute power to build next generation models rather than service current clients. I will assume an end-mix of 75% of revenues from premium products, and 25% from the mass market, giving me an unadjusted pre-tax operating margin of 32.5%; that would put them at the ninth decile of US companies in 2026.  

     Here again, you may find room for disagreement, either on the market mix (mass market versus premium), the margins for each market segment or business economics, as companies scale up. You can make your choice below: 

 Again, my estimate of the target margin is highlighted in black, but with plenty of room for a different choice.

 3. The Reinvestment Story 
     The reinvestment assumptions you make for Anthropic will revolve around understanding compute power, in terms of both how it is created as well as how much frontier models will need that power, as they become more powerful and scale up. For the moment, Anthropic, with its compute commitments in excess of $600 billion and greater, has sent signals that it views compute power as a necessity to power its growth ambitions as well as to maintain an edge over competitors (current and prospective). 

     The nature of compute power, and especially with the chips that represent a large percentage of costs, is that investments will age quickly and will need replacement. This is an indication that if Anthropic's growth ambitions come to fruition, there will be more reinvestment needed in future years, to both replenish and grow compute power. It is true that technology may make chips cheaper, but that may be more than offset by new models demanding proportionately more power, and if you add in the real estate and power needs of data centers, there is room for diverge on how much additional investment will be needed in future years. I do believe that the compute power crunch will stay in place for the near term, but will ease over time, and that belief translates into my assumption that Anthropic will need to invest about $1 for every $3 in additional revenues, going forward. That would be in line with what technology companies are generating as revenues per dollar of invested capital today, but with the leap in revenues that Anthropic is forecasting, it will translate into large dollar reinvestments each year. 

     As with revenue growth and profitability, I will leave the door open for disagreement, and you can make your choice below:

 While I have highlighted my base case assumption in black, note that lower sales to capital ratios will make the business more capital-intensive, and increase the cash drain from reinvestment. 
 4. The Risk Story 
     As you start listing out the risks that you will be exposed to as an Anthropic investor, you may be overwhelmed both by the number of risks as well as their diversity. To gain some control in this process, I will divide the risks into three groups: 

 a. Operating risk: The AI business is still evolving, and while Anthropic's growth and customer stickiness so far are noteworthy, the business will face challenges as it grows, and lives through market and economic turmoil. Thus, for Anthropic's customers spending on AI as a productivity tool, we do not know whether they will cut back their spending, and if so how much, in bad times, and for those who plan to replace employees with AI agents, whether the pace and extent of usage will change with the economy. The number that is designed to convey this risk into the valuation is the cost of capital, and for Anthropic, assuming that it carries the risk of large technology companies with an added burden of the compute commitments, I will estimate a cost of capital of 9.74%. Again, for perspective, note that the median cost of capital for US firms in September 2026 was 9.16% and that the third quartile for US firms is 9.88% . If you disagree, here are your choices:

 My advice, and feel free to ignore it, is that you should not spend too much time finessing the cost of capital, since of the many assumptions that drive this valuation, it is among the least critical. While I highlight my base case cost of capital, remember that when investing in a publicly traded company, what you would like to use as a cost of capital has to be constrained by what the market is offering. 
 b. Financing risk:  The main talking point for many Anthropic bears is the compute commitment that runs into hundreds of billions, creating fixed costs that will be a drag on profitability, especially if revenue growth falls short of expectations, as well as the risk of distress. While bondholders are right to be trepidatious and will point to the current bond rating of BB+ for the company as backing for their concerns, there are two reasons why failure risk will be suppressed. The first is that the company has the cash balance to sustain itself through the near terms and meet its contractual obligations. The second is that, as a high-profile trillion-dollar plus publicly traded company, it will have access to capital. I do believe, though, that if revenues grow at anemic rates, both these benefits will dissipate, as cash gets burned through and the market cap collapses, and I will estimate a probability of failure of 10% for the company, with a loss of half its value if that happen.  If you want to disagree, go into the input sheet worksheet of the spreadsheet , and if you scroll down

items.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
items.content:
I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus  of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies.  While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs), rather than with total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows.

 Young Companies in a Corporate Life Cycle 
      All businesses, no matter how large and established they might be today, started as young businesses and matured. With that perspective in mind, I will start this discussion by placing young businesses in a corporate life cycle in the figure below:

One of the first steps in analyzing a company is placing it in the right stage of the life cycle, and there are three choices that you can use in making this placement:
 Chronological age : The first and simplest choice is to look at the age of a business, putting companies that have been in operation for short periods into the young company grouping and classifying those that have been in operation for longer as mature. While this approach is easy to use, and for the most part, effective, it can be misleading in businesses like infrastructure, where it can take decades to get established, and in technology, where the lack of capital intensity can allow a company can go from start-up to mature in a few years. Industry grouping : Another choice is categorizing industry groups into life cycle stages and assuming that any company that belongs to a specific industry group shares its life cycle characteristics. For decades, investors have viewed technology as a shorthand for growth and put technology companies into the earlier stages of the life cycle and utilities as mature or even declining and put all utility companies into the mature to declining company grouping. The limitation of this approach is that there will be divergence within each group, where some companies separate themselves from their industry group; there are mature and even declining companies that are in the technology grouping, and there are power companies that have taken advantage of the data center boom to become growth companies. With technology in particular, where companies age in dog years, I talked about how companies can get mis-categorized and sometimes mismanaged as growth companies , even though their best days are behind them.  Operating metrics : Ultimately, life cycle effects show up in the operating metrics of companies, and there are common characteristics that young companies share, and they include the following: High revenue growth : Young companies usually have high revenue growth, and while this is usually off a small revenue base, there are exceptions, where companies with scaled up revenues are still able to show high growth. Operating losses : As young companies scale up, they usually struggle with unformed business models, and at low scale, their fixed costs overwhelm their revenues, resulting in negative or very low operating profit margins. Negative free cash flows : Free cash flows are after reinvestment, and as young companies invest to deliver on their potential growth, that reinvestment will generate negative free cash flows. Failure risk : The confluence of small revenues, losses and negative free cashflows, which must be funded with external capital (equity or debt) exposes young firms to significant risk of failure. The figure below captures the shifts in operating metrics, as companies move through the life cycle:

 Put simply, if a company has revenue growth in single digits, stable margins and positive free cash flows to the firm, it is a mature company, no matter how it views itself. Conversely, a firm with high revenue growth, negative or very low profit margins and large negative free cashflows to the firms is a young growth firm, no matter what its scale. Recognizing those characteristics is critical in understanding why so many give up on valuing young companies, and why pricing will often be based on unfamiliar metrics.

     How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up in the life cycle? Using a patchwork of public data and leaked information, here are the numbers on key operating metrics that I have as of October 2026 for both companies: 

 The sky-high revenue growth and operating losses are a clear indication that these are young, growth companies, but note that the revenues (albeit on an ARR basis) at both companies are already large, suggesting that they are growing at scale. That should come as no surprise, since they are both rumored to be looking at IPOs in excess of a trillion dollars, in terms of total market capitalization. The business models are still in flux in both companies, as they wrestle with how best to structure their business models (usage versus subscription) and struggle with market targeting questions (premium versus mass market). I know that Anthropic claimed to be profitable in the second quarter of 2026, but I don't think that even Anthropic believes this to be true, since these are adjusted profits and the adjustments represent a patchwork of add-backs of legitimate expenses. As for cash flows, both Anthropic and OpenAI are deep in the hole, with negative free cash flows, at the moment, and whether they are able to generate positive cash flows in the future is entirely a function of how the AI business evolves over time.

 Pricing versus Valuation: Across the life cycle 
     I will start with a distinction that I believe needs to be made between two approaches to attaching numbers to assets and businesses. The first is to value that asset or business, based on its capacity to generate and grow cash flows, and the risk in those cashflows, i.e., intrinsic valuation. The second is to price that asset or business by looking at what others are paying for "similar' assets, thus reducing pricing to demand and supply. The picture below captures that difference:

 It is true that if you believed in efficient markets, price would converge on value, but if you did, you would save yourself the time and aggravation associated with trying to price or value assets by investing in index funds, and moving on to more productive pursuits. If you don't believe in efficient markets, you can take one of two paths. You can take the investor route ,  trying to value assets and businesses, with the intent of buying undervalued and/or selling overvalued companies, and hoping that price converges on value. Alternatively, you can take the trading path , where you throw up your hands on intrinsic value, arguing that it is too subjective and difficult to estimate, and make your money by buying investments at low prices and selling them at higher prices,  using whatever tools (including charts and technical indicators) you want to use, to make your judgments. 
     While you can value and price any business, there are reasons why the usage of each can vary depending upon where a company is in the life cycle. To value a business, you have to estimate expected future cash flows, and to make these estimates of cash flows, growth and risk, and you generally draw on three sources of information: 

 Financial statements : The current financial statements of a company provide information on unit economics, profitability and risk, and historical financial statements are useful in assessing growth in the business and changes in business profitability. For mature businesses that have been in operating for long period, much or even all of what you need to value the company can be in its financial statements, but for younger companies, the current financials may not yield much (as growth and unformed business models create noise) and there is little history, Market size and growth : Knowing the size of the total market that a company is aiming for, and how quickly it is growing can help put reasonability constraints on the growth rate and market you estimate for a company. For companies in established markets, this should be relatively easy to do, but for companies in new and evolving markets, this can become difficult. Industry statistics : As you forecast profit margins and the risk profile for a company, having that information for the crosssection of companies in the industry can establish bounds and help in making estimates. If you frame an intrinsic valuation in terms of the big estimation questions that need to be addressed to arrive at value, starting with the cash flows from existing investments, moving on to estimating the value that will be added by future growth and assessing risk, you can see that valuing young companies will always be more complicated than valuing more mature businesses. In fact, looking at Anthropic and OpenAI, you can see why valuation will be daunting:

 While I am a glutton for punishment, and I will try, albeit with error, to make my best judgments on Anthropic's future cash flows, risk and value (as I did with SpaceX), when the prospectus is made public, I understand why most will turn away in the face of uncertainty and choose not to value the company. Some of these investors will also look at how those that they believe know more about that companies are assessing its value, and peruse prior venture capital rounds at both Anthropic and OpenAI for clues on value.  Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been active in raising equity as private companies, and the most recent rounds yield estimates of what these private investors thought they were worth, at least at the time the capital was raised. The table below summarizes the number of VC rounds, with capital raised, at both companies, as well as the pricing in their most recent rounds:

 Anthropic's VC round in May 2026 , from a cross section of big-name venture capitalists, raised $65 billion for the company, at a post-money pricing of $965 billion .   OpenAI's most recent capital raise was in March 2026, when it raised $122 billion, at a post-money pricing for the company at $852 billion . OpenAI also has a pending round of capital raise ahead of an IPO, where they expect to raise $30 billion with a pricing for the company of roughly $1.4 trillion .  

      While you may be tempted to assume that the VC pricing in these rounds are rooted in value, venture capitalists are in the pricing game, as I have argued in prior posts , In fact, they, stretch pricing metrics and definitions of peer groups, and VC valuation is almost always forward pricing :

 In the case of Anthropic and OpenAI, this forward pricing process is both more compressed and even less informative than at most young companies, with investors viewing the companies as imminent IPOs, and pricing them based upon their expectations of the pricing of the public offering, and discounting that expected price for negative surprises about the company's prospects that may lower the pricing or delay/cancel the IPO:

 The expected pricing will be a function of pricing in prior VC rounds, management wishlists and even rumors, and the discount applied will increase as the time to the IPO lengthens and with the uncertainties about the company and its potential market. For Anthropic, for instance, at the time of the VC round, the expected pricing for the IPO was $1.15 trillion, well below what the expectations are today, and reflective of how much can change over short periods with young companies, and the $965 billion pricing in the VC round would have represented a $150 billion discount on the estimate.

 Pricing Process 
      While the reluctance to value young companies, and fall back to pricing is understandable, I would push back on the notion that doing so dispenses with the need to make the assumptions about cashflows, growth and risk that are required in intrinsic valuation. In this section, I will break down the pricing process into steps, and look at the issues that you faced when valuing these companies also create impediments in pricing, and in the next section, why using a multiple of annualized revenue run rates (ARR) or even eyeballs makes implicit assumptions about future profitability, growth and reinvestment. 

 The Steps in the Process 
     If, in pricing, you attach a number to an asset or business, based upon what others are paying for similar assets or business, how exactly does this process play out when valuing a company or business? No matter who does the pricing, and how sophisticated they claim to be, there are three steps in pricing companies:

 Standardize the price : The nature of pricing shares in public markets is that the share price is a function of share count, which is arbitrary; a stock split for instance halves the price while doubling the count and total market capitalization or value is a function of company size. To allow for comparisons across companies, you standardize the market price by dividing by a common variable that you can obtain for each of the companies in your comparison, with the choices ranging from revenues (or revenue drivers) to earnings to cashflow variants to book value. Since the market price can be for just equity (market capitalization) or for the entire business (enterprise value, which includes net debt), the denominator has to be defined in the same terms, with equity (operating) income and book value of equity (invested capital) going with market capitalization (enterprise value). Find peer group companies : For pricing to be functional, you have to find other priced companies just like the one that you are pricing. The simplistic solution is to start with other companies in the same industry or business grouping, with added constraints on geography and company size thrown in. Needless to say, even if done with care, the choice of companies in the peer group is subjective and can vary across analysts and investors, even when looking at the same company. Control for differences : No mater what pricing metric (PE, EV to Sales etc.) you pick, there will be fundamental reasons why companies will trade at different values, and for a pricing to have substance, you have to control for differences. Thus, if PE ratio is your metric, a company that expects higher growth in earnings or lower risk than its peer group, should trade at a higher PE ratio than the peer group does, and that difference has to enter your discussion. The picture below captures these steps, with the variants on pricing metrics and the considerations in peer group construction included:

 While this process remains the same for every pricing, there are reasons why pricing metrics will vary across companies and why peer group construction may be easier in some cases than other, and I will take Anthropic and OpenAI through the process.

1. Pricing metrics 
     With some companies, your choice of pricing metrics will span the spectrum, with revenues, earnings, cash flows and book value all competing as scalars. However, your choices will narrow at others, and one reason that is relevant to the Anthropic/OpenAI discussion is where a company falls in the life cycle:

 As you can see, early in the life cycle, when companies are losing money, have negative free cashflows and little tangible capital invested in assets in place, you will see revenue often as the only viable metric, leading to revenue multiples dominating the discourse. Put simply, desperation drives you up the income statement until you find a positive number. It should be no surprise, therefore, that the metric that companies and investors have focused on with Anthropic and OpenAI is revenues . Those revenues are growing so quickly at these companies, that their argument is that trailing numbers are dated by the time hey are released, and that has led to the shift to annualized revenue run rates (where using revenues from the last week or month allows for more updated vales). As we noted earlier, the perils with annualized revenue rates (ARR) is that they are not standardized and can be easily gamed. Just in the last few weeks, there have been news stories on the divergence between gross and net revenues with OpenAI shifting towards using the latter, lowering ARR from $70 billion to $50 billion, while Anthropic continues to report gross revenues and the cloud provider payments as expenses. In addition, you can compute ARR using the last day's, the last week's and the last month's revenues, and while Anthropic and OpenAI have both converged on monthly annualization, there is nothing that binds them to continue to do so. 

     There is a second choice that will come into play as the debate about Anthropic's pricing becomes more heated, and that is whether to use revenues in a future period, i.e.. forward revenue . By forecasting the annualized revenue run rate of $100 billion plus by the end of 2026, Anthropic has already opened the door, but do not be surprised if investors and analysts shift to looking at revenues in 2030 or 2036, since scaling prices today to forward revenues five or ten years out will make the pricing multiple look lower, and thus more defensible. Once you decide to go forward in time, it is plausible that you can even shift to expected earnings in 2031 or 2036, built around expected operating or net profit margins; arguing that Anthropic is cheap because it trades (today) at 25 times 2036 earnings (based on your estimated revenues and net margins) brings the multiple back to earth, but at what cost? Investors use frames of what comprises normal or high, based  upon their acquaintance with a multiple, and many will (mistakenly) compare these forwards earnings multiples to current earnings multiples in the market to make their investment judgment on cheap or expensive. 
     There is a third choice, and that is to relate the pricing of these companies to a variable that you believe will be correlated with future revenues and earnings. With that choice, you can see the rationale for estimating enterprise value per user or subscriber for user and subscriber based companies, with the connector being the logic that more users and subscribers today is a leading indicator of higher revenues and earnings in the future. It was that logic that led Mary Meeker and other internet analysts to use website visitors and eyeballs in pricing dot com companies, and while you may disagree, the logic holds.
